hook: Your brain physically cannot tell the difference between planning and doing. That's a problem.
topic: The planning paradox — how over-planning is procrastination
body:
**Your brain physically cannot tell the difference between planning and doing. And that is exactly the problem.**

When you plan a task in enough detail — when you map the steps, think through the approach, organise the framework — your brain releases a mild reward signal. It treats the mental simulation of the work as partial progress. Which means you've been paid before you've done anything.

This is why high-performers are especially susceptible to planning as procrastination. The planning feels like work. It requires thought. It produces something — a document, a system, a to-do list. But the actual output hasn't moved.

There is a point at which additional planning produces negative returns — where the next unit of preparation costs more than it contributes, and what you need instead is imperfect execution.

The reframe: if you've planned it more than once, you don't need a better plan. You need a worse start. An imperfect beginning beats a perfect plan that never launches.

One action: set a rule — any task you've planned more than twice gets a forced start within 24 hours, with whatever information you currently have. Imperfect and moving beats complete and static every time.
